newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. may appeal against judge's extradition block.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may appeal against judge's extradition block.

text.p: The United States government said on Thursday it was considering an appeal against a district court judge's ruling which blocks the extradition of a fugitive to Hong Kong.

In a statement issued by the American consulate in Hong Kong, the U.S. also said it stood by an extradition agreement signed recently with Hong Kong and trusted the territory would keep its judicial independence after reverting to Chinese rule on July 1.
"The United States government disagrees with the decision. We understand that the U.S. Justice Department is considering whether to appeal," the statement said.

Boston District Court Judge Joseph Tauro made a decision on Tuesday blocking the extradition of suspect Jerry Lui Kin-hong, who faces multi-million dollar bribery and conspiracy charges in Hong Kong relating to cigarette smuggling.
Lui had argued he faced possible execution if forced to return to Hong Kong because his trial was unlikely to be completed before the handover to China on July 1.

But the judge's decision, seen as undermining Hong Kong's efforts to convince the world it would retain its judicial independence after it reverts to China's rule, sparked a furore in the territory and triggered an urgent appeal from the Hong Kong government.

The ruling also raised questions over an agreement signed last month between the United States and Hong Kong preventing the surrender of fugitives to a third jurisdiction such as China, ensuring they remained in Hong Kong.
But in its statement the U.S. said it would stand by the extradition agreement.

"We are comfortable with extradition to Hong Kong both now and in the future...we have recently signed an extradition agreement with the Hong Kong government that would remain in force after July 1997," it said.
"We believe this agreement will serve the overall interests of the United States, allowing the continued extradition to the U.S. of criminals, including narcotics traffickers," it said.
The statement said the United States recognised that Hong Kong would maintain a separate regime from China in judicial matters as provided for in Sino-British handover treaties.
"The Sino-British Joint Declaration clearly provides for Hong Kong to maintain its criminal justice, judicial and penal system separate and distinct from China's," it said.
